C0.quote: game-theoretic considerations when voters are allowed to trade votes
C0.note: Vote trading under majority rule on two binary issues; strategic equilibrium analysis of a voting procedure.

C1.quote: We compute the Nash equilibria for this game
C1.note: Nash equilibrium characterisation (Theorem 1, existence) is the core. Group welfare is evaluated as sum of utilities. Section 3 applies the model to ANES survey data. The numerical examples are synthetic computations, not simulations of agents.

C2.1.quote: voters cast their votes on both issues

C2.2.quote: utilities on both issues which can take any value between −1 and 1
C2.2.note: Voters hold cardinal utilities on two issues. The submitted input is a yes/no vote on each binary issue (OTH), plus a trade offer.

C2.3.quote: voters are independently assigned utilities on both issues

C2.4.quote: the other n − 2 voters will vote sincerely
C2.4.note: Utilities (held) and trade offers/votes (submitted) are separate objects. Non-trading votes are sincere by assumption, and trade offers are strategic.

C3.1.quote: making myopic decisions as if no other voters will make trades
C3.1.note: Trade offers are strategic, but final votes on issues are cast sincerely. Trading actions are strategic in all analyses, so whether voting itself is strategic is ambiguous. Pick SOME.

C3.2.note: Statement about sincere voting for others: 'the other n − 2 voters will vote sincerely'.

C3.3.quote: as if no other voters will make trades (Casella and Palfrey 2018)
C3.3.note: Myopic or sincere behaviour is justified by a citation and a modelling simplification only.

C4.1.note: The input format is not ordinal or approval. Utilities are primitive.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.quote: we define the welfare of the group to be the sum
C5.1.note: Group welfare is the sum of utilities. It is evaluated in results and in the real-data analysis.

C5.2.quote: the sum of the voters’ final utilities
C5.2.note: Welfare is evaluated on held utilities defined separately from the votes.

VOT.quote_behav: our voters are short-sighted, making myopic decisions
VOT.quote_info: incomplete information about the preferences of their partners
VOT.note: Traders choose trade offers strategically (Nash equilibrium). Non-trading voters vote sincerely. Voters know the utility distribution but not partners' utilities. The Discussion says voters have 'complete information about the preferences of the entire group', which is inconsistent with the model.

DES.note: The cost-imposition remark in Section 2.2 is informal and does not model a designer's choice.

C7.1.note: Only the voter type is present.

C8.1.quote: we restrict ourselves to non-trivial equilibria
C8.1.note: Nash equilibria of the vote trading game.

C8.2.quote: We compute the Nash equilibria for this game

claims.quote: trades are typically detrimental to the welfare of the group as a whole
two voters trading votes on real issues is probably harming group welfare
vote trading adds value for the entire group infrequently, at best

C9.1.note: Claims about real vote trading and group welfare.

C9.2.quote: estimate the joint probability distribution of American voter utilities
C9.2.note: The real-world welfare claim needs a statement that ANES preference-intensity responses equal voters' true utilities on [-1,1]. The mapping from the 1-7 survey scale to utilities is not stated. It also needs the assumption that real voters behave as in the myopic, incomplete-information model. The claim also needs the assumption that real legislators trade one-for-one and without information about each other. The paper states the information and myopia assumptions but not the utility mapping.
